1:
Henry sets the chapter under the second commandment, that from the truths that there is a God and but one God arise the laws that he only is to be worshipped and that we may not worship him as the false gods were worshipped, the second commandment being a hedge about the first. He presses the two notes of time, that the statutes bind in prosperity as well as in the wilderness, and all the days we live upon the earth. Keil and Delitzsch describe the opening more architecturally, that the second half of the address now begins and will regulate the ecclesiastical, civil and domestic life of Israel in Canaan. Gill and Ellicott summarise its demands, and Clarke sets out the whole sequence from the destruction of the monuments to the closing prohibition against adding to the word of God.

Henry observes that no idol temples are mentioned, which supports those who think the tabernacle the first building ever raised for religious use. He explains why the high places and green trees were chosen, height being thought to help devotion and shade to compose the mind, but adds that their real advantage was to conceal works of darkness which could not bear the light. Wesley glosses the places as temples, chapels and altars, and Keil and Delitzsch read the verses as a command to sweep away every trace.

Clarke identifies the altars as places of unholy sacrifice, the pillars as statues cut from stone, the groves as enclosures like those about the temple of Ashtaroth, and the graven images as figures carved in wood. On the destroying of the names he observes that these were graven on stones and thence passed to the country round, whole mountains and valleys taking their names from the gods worshipped there. Ellicott supplies a striking instance of literal fulfilment, that baal was later replaced by bosheth in Jerubbaal, Eshbaal and Meribbaal, though he thinks it may answer rather to the parallel in Exodus. Gill and Wesley take the pillars for the supports on which images stood.

Ellicott meets the objection that the command belongs to a later age because early Israel did not fulfil it, arguing that its execution was bound up with the conquest in detail, Joshua breaking the armies and leaving each tribe to cleanse its own territory. Had every tribe insisted on it, he reasons, either the remnant would have rebelled and been exterminated or they must have yielded wholly to the worship of Jehovah; and Israel's failure was not from any leaning to idolatry, as the alarm over the altar Ed shows. Gill reports the rabbinic reading of the next verse, that while heathen altars were to be overthrown not a stone might be taken from the house of God nor any of his names blotted out, Maimonides adding that whoever removes one by way of destruction is beaten. Ellicott takes the verse more simply, that they were not to serve the Lord in that manner.

Keil and Delitzsch draw out the contrast, that where the heathen seeks nature-gods wherever he discerns a trace of divinity, the true God has revealed not only his power in creation but his personal being in the works of salvation, and has fixed a name in which he dwells among his people. That name, they add, presents his personality in a visible pledge of his presence, which during the journeying was the pillar of cloud and fire. Calvin states the same as the chief external distinction between lawful worship and the fictitious Gentile rites, that God would have but one sanctuary and one altar, a symbol of the difference between himself and every idol. A barrier was thus raised, he concludes, to separate the people from the world, and the external profession of worship is fitly annexed to the second commandment.
5:
Henry observes that no precept in all the law is so largely pressed as this, and gives three reasons: the proneness of that people to idolatry, the usefulness of one place to keep corrupt customs out of worship and preserve unity, and the significancy of the appointment, which he takes for a token that there is one God and one Mediator between God and man. This bound the sacrifices and rituals only, he adds, since as to moral services men might pray everywhere then as now, as in their synagogues. Wesley says the same more briefly.

Calvin asks why sacrifice was confined to one altar, and answers that God had regard to believers, cherishing an agreement in the unity of faith, so that the place stood like a standard to gather the people lest religion be torn by divisions, and that by reserving the choice to himself he commended the obedience on which purity of worship depends. Since the ark had no fixed resting-place before David, the people would seem free meanwhile to sacrifice where they pleased; he answers that the place was not chosen till the ark was set in Zion, and presses out of all your tribes as marking a privilege given to one tribe and withheld from the rest, citing the psalm in which God refused the tabernacle of Joseph and chose Judah and Mount Zion. Ellicott takes the same words the opposite way: the form of the order proves its antiquity, since no one acquainted with the removal of the place from Shiloh to Nob, to Gibeon and thence to Jerusalem could have written with such unconsciousness of later history.

The Jews of our Lord's time, he adds, could not conceive of the worship of Jehovah anywhere but at Jerusalem, and he refers to Stephen's speech for its incidental proofs of God's presence with Israel in many places. Keil and Delitzsch attend instead to the gifts, classing them in four pairs, the sacrifices proper with their meat and drink offerings, the tithes of field-produce and cattle with every heave-offering of the hand, and argue that the tithes meant are not the vegetable tithes only. Gill enumerates the same offerings; Wesley explains to put his name there as setting up his worship in a house called by his name, first at Shiloh, afterwards at Jerusalem.

On the eating before the Lord Calvin says the sanctuary was where God manifested himself present, so the meal was a communion and not a mere feast; Wesley guards it, that the eating was not in the most holy place but in the courts. Keil and Delitzsch call the sacrificial meals the visible expression of the joy of a people admitted to God's table. Henry dwells on the gladness, that the service was a pleasure and not a task, and they were to rejoice with their households; Gill observes from the mention of daughters that women too came up to the feasts.

Ellicott finds in they shall not do as they do here this day another mark of the wilderness condition, and insists that the law has a prophetic side, given when Israel was not in a position to keep it, its observance waiting on the conquest and on quiet times; the Jews themselves did not dwell in booths at the Feast of Tabernacles from Joshua's day to Nehemiah's. He reports Rashi on the giving of rest. Calvin holds that the promise of rest following confirms his reading of the chosen place. Clarke closes by explaining why uniformity was then essential: every rite had a determinate meaning and pointed to things to come, so that without one place the representative system would have been destroyed and the Messiah could not have been seen through the Jewish ritual. The same necessity does not now exist, the shadows having fled, though it remains desirable that Christians should glorify their Lord with one mouth.
15:
The one place settled, the law relieves it of the common table. Gill notes that they might kill cattle allowed for food and eat the flesh in their own cities, no longer obliged to bring them to the sanctuary as in the wilderness. Ellicott takes the verse as a deliberate modification of Leviticus 17:3-4, where killing an ox or lamb or goat is forbidden anywhere but at the tabernacle door: continuing that precept in Canaan would have stopped the eating of flesh altogether, whence the exception. Calvin reads it the same way, provided they do not offer the animals to God but eat them as wild beasts, the roebuck and hart being kinds of which no offering was made. Clarke thinks the roebuck an antelope and the hart a deer on Dr Shaw's authority, and reasons that since game is shot with arrows, its blood not being poured at the altar, the command concerns only tame beasts used for food; the frequent mention of these animals, Ellicott adds, suggests hunting was familiar in the wilderness.

One thing only is reserved. Gill takes the prohibition at its widest, of fowl or beast, slain for sacrifice or for common food. Keil and Delitzsch note that the blood was poured on the earth like water, that it might suck it in and receive it into its bosom. Clarke resists Calmet's reading that pouring it as water means pouring it with as little ceremony as water, holding rather that it was poured by way of sacrifice. Calvin treats the point at length: the abstinence was commanded to Noah but had fallen into desuetude, so God ratifies it anew as a mark of separation from the heathen; its reason is that the blood is the life, and its use a restraint upon inhumanity, since men who spare the blood of beasts will much more spare human blood, which is why the words following in Genesis pass at once to whoso sheddeth man's blood. Eating blood is in itself of no great weight, he observes, and the severity of the punishment shows a further object, that cruelty might be abhorred; against Augustine, who read the blood is the life as the sign of life, he holds that Moses means animal life is contained in the blood. Ellicott makes the pouring out a necessary part of every slaughter for food, a reminder of the death of Christ, and in that sense sacramental.

The holy things are excepted from the licence. Gill argues that the tithe forbidden is not the Levites' portion, which only they ate, but the tithe laid up within the gates every third year, the other two years carried to the chosen place or turned into money and spent there. Ellicott reports that Jewish commentators understand the second tithe, its disposal specified in Deuteronomy 14:22-29; Wesley glosses within thy gates as the private habitations, set over against the place of God's worship. Keil and Delitzsch state the rule plainly, that sacrificial meals belonged to the sanctuary alone and the Levite was not to be forgotten in them; Gill adds that these were eaten before the Lord in the sense of being eaten where his sanctuary stood.

The section closes with the Levite. Ellicott sees their distribution through the tribes anticipated here, ordered in Numbers 35 and carried out by Joshua, and notes that they kept this provision until Jeroboam cast them off and they migrated to Judah. Gill takes forsaking to mean withholding the tithes appointed for his maintenance or, as he prefers, neglecting to take him to the entertainment just described. Clarke puts it sharpest: the Levites had no inheritance and lived by the sanctuary, so if the offerings were withheld they must perish; those who devote themselves to God's service should be furnished at least with the necessaries of life, and those who withhold it sin against their own mercies.
20:
The permission of verse 15 is restated with its reason. Gill takes the enlarging of the border of the entry into Canaan, where they would have good pastures and a greater increase of cattle than the wilderness allowed. Ellicott reads verses 20 to 25 as an expansion of 15 and 16 and a modification of the strict Levitical rule, the distance from the central place of worship to the borders of the land being plainly too great for all feasting to be confined there. Wesley makes the point twice, that an enlarged border would make it impossible to bring all their cattle to the tabernacle, and that men obliged to carry their sacrifices thither might think themselves bound to carry the rest too, the release being given to quiet that scruple; only the far case is mentioned, he notes, because that was the matter of the scruple, though the liberty holds near and far alike. Gill presses the particle, reading if the place be too far as rather seeing it will be too far.

The measure of the licence is the game already allowed. Gill observes that the roebuck and hart were not only clean but commonly eaten, being plentiful in those parts. Keil and Delitzsch state the rule exactly, that flesh merely slaughtered was eaten as the hart and roebuck, not made into a sacrifice, and gloss the word rendered alike as together, the one just as the other, without implying that the clean must eat with the unclean. Wesley agrees that they were eaten as common or unhallowed food though of the same kind as the sacrifices, and that the unclean were not excluded because there was no holiness in such meat.

The one exception is repeated with emphasis, Gill noting that it is said again that they might be careful to observe it. Keil and Delitzsch render the imperative literally, be strong not to eat the blood, that is, stedfastly resist the temptation, and Calvin explains why so earnest an exhortation to firmness was needed: the thing was trifling in appearance and troublesome to keep, and the universal example of the Gentiles made it easy to decline from, so that if a man reasoned that not touching blood contributed nothing to holiness, a snare to indulgence might arise. Clarke gives the reason from Leviticus, that the blood is the life and the life was offered as an atonement. Gill adds the sanction, that God threatened to set his face against blood-eaters and cut them off, while the promise here is that they and their posterity might be spared and continue long; Ellicott suggests that the physical as well as the moral effect of the rule may be contemplated in it.

The holy things remain reserved. Gill reports that Onkelos and Jonathan take the holy things of the tithe, Aben Ezra of the burnt and peace offerings, and thinks the term includes all named earlier; Ellicott judges that they probably mean the firstlings, necessarily holy and to be made burnt offerings, with the second tithe reckoned holy but the first, the ordinary provision for the Levites, not, and the vows either burnt or peace offerings. Keil and Delitzsch note that vows are joined to the holy gifts because they proceeded from a spontaneous impulse. Ellicott identifies the sacrifices whose blood was poured at the altar as the peace offerings, the only kind of which the worshipper as well as the priest might partake, and Wesley excepts what was burned to God's honour and given to the priest. Calvin sums the whole: one place was set apart lest, if each offered where he pleased, religion should be corrupted and the various altars beget as many gods. On the closing promise he warns that the hope of reward does not of itself arouse men, but that God indulges believers by promising it because their innumerable defects are not imputed.
29:
The address returns at the close to where it began, the idolatry of the land. Keil and Delitzsch describe the movement exactly: the warning against Canaanite idolatry is a transition from the true worship of Jehovah to the laws about tempters to idolatry in chapter 13. Gill identifies the nations as the seven of Canaan and reads the snare as their examples and customs; Wesley puts it sharper, that the danger is the example they left when their persons were destroyed. Calvin holds that Moses does not mean the nations were enslaved by right of capture but speaks of the land: when they are destroyed it lies vacant. He records renderings of the verb of the snare that suit the construction better, but keeps the received one for the aptness of the metaphor, the perversities of the Gentiles being nets to entrap men who come too near.

The prohibition falls not on the practice only but on the enquiry. Calvin makes this his chief observation: it is easy to pass from one to the other, and here is the origin of idolatry, when the simplicity of God's worship is known and men grow dissatisfied and ask whether the figments of men hold anything worthy of belief, minds being soon caught by novelty. God therefore does not merely restrain enquiry but bids them take heed to themselves, since men are naturally disposed to this curiosity; he encloses his people with barriers and would have them so abominate superstitions as to fly the very infection of hearing of them. Ellicott confirms the caution from later history: the fear of heathen deities often attached to their seats of worship, and Israel was still warned against the dread of them in Jeremiah.

The reason given is the character of the rites. Keil and Delitzsch summarise it, that the Canaanites prepare all kinds of abominations for their gods which Jehovah abhors, and even burn their children to their idols, as to Moloch; Gill concludes that Israel was not to serve the Lord after the manner of the Gentiles nor bring their rites into his service. Calvin gathers what it is not to make oneself the gods of others: to bid farewell to the inventions of men and attend to what God commands. There ought to be a notable distinction lest religion be confused, and unless men resolve that nothing is permitted but what his word teaches, they will receive whatever comes their way. God does not only repudiate these worships but abominates them, and the form adduced is chosen because its absurdity is manifest, it being a foul barbarity that innocent children should be burnt by their parents. Clarke enlarges on that: almost all nations offered human victims on extraordinary occasions, which shows that none had any right notion of the divine nature, and proves how necessary revelation was to teach men what religion pleases God.

The closing clause is read as a rule of worship. Gill takes it that the laws were to be obeyed as delivered, in matter and manner, adding nothing from heathen custom and neglecting nothing enjoined. Keil and Delitzsch note that many make the verse the conclusion of the preceding chapter, but judge it rather an intermediate link, closing what goes before and introducing what follows. Ellicott finds an argument for authorship: no later writer could have put these words in the mouth of Moses if he had himself altered the precepts appreciably. Calvin makes it the summary of the whole: no service of God is lawful but that of which he has testified his approval in his word, obedience being the mother of piety, so that whatever men invent is condemned and those guided by any other rule make themselves false gods. He cites the threatening in Isaiah against those who draw near by the precept of men, and applies it without reserve to the Papal ceremonies.
